claims.claim: A portfolio is a curated collection of a designer's work and is the primary basis on which graphic designers are evaluated: candidates for design positions are expected to demonstrate their creativity and originality through a portfolio, even though designers typically also hold a bachelor's degree.

Employers of graphic-design graduates increasingly prioritise general employability skills (communication, collaboration, problem-solving) alongside disciplinary and technical craft, so a portfolio must evidence both; 'portfolio literacy' combines curation of the portfolio with its use in interview performance.

Effective curation means selecting a smaller set of the strongest and most relevant pieces (quality over quantity) and tailoring the selection to the target role, rather than including everything; focus on standout pieces that align with career goals.

A portfolio piece should be presented as a case study that contextualises the work with the challenge/problem faced, the approach and decisions, and the outcome, documenting the design process rather than showing only a final image.

The professional design process begins by defining the project's goals and researching the problem before concepts are developed and solutions implemented; a case study makes this otherwise-invisible process visible.

A portfolio is itself a designed object judged by design standards, and is commonly delivered as an online personal website and/or in formats prepared for print, digital, and web, with clarity and consistent presentation part of what is evaluated.
Professional portfolio practice requires crediting collaborators and highlighting group work (stating one's own role) and maintaining professionalism when presenting work to employers.

Career context: graphic designers had a median annual wage of $61,300 (May 2024), employment is projected to grow about 2 percent from 2024 to 2034, and the typical entry-level education is a bachelor's degree.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Recommended portfolio size varies across sources (e.g., a handful of standout pieces vs. 8-20 projects).
positions: University career guidance suggests focusing on a few standout pieces (e.g., 1-3 highlighted) aligned to career goals.
Industry guides commonly suggest roughly 8-20 projects for a full portfolio.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids asserting a single 'correct' number and teaches the underlying principle instead: quality over quantity and relevance to the target role. No specific count is stated as a rule.

sourceRecords.title: Portfolio Literacy and the Transition to Work for Graphic Design Graduates
sourceRecords.provider: International Journal of Art & Design Education (Barnes, Wragg, Fisher, Tyagi, de Kruiff)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed article (2022), CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (license and full metadata verified via the Crossref API record for DOI 10.1111/jade.12407 on 2026-08-19; the Wiley page itself returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher). Abstract (verified verbatim via Crossref) reports a survey of 53 Australian employers of graphic-design graduates and argues graduates need 'portfolio literacy', combining curation of the portfolio with its use in interview performance, to demonstrate both core graphic-design skills and general capacities in communication, collaboration and problem-solving, and notes employers may prioritise generic over disciplinary/technical skills. Because NoDerivatives forbids adapted redistribution, treated as REFERENCE_ONLY: findings paraphrased, no text reproduced.
